To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the airways are colonized by bacteria and fungi that can be altered in disease, the microbiota can influence lung function and host responses, and host–microbiota interactions can influence the course of lung disease.
the airway microbiome is an important component of lung health, and that dysbiosis of this microbiome can contribute to the development and progression of lung diseases.

we have identified a novel role for the microbiota in regulating host responses to inhaled pathogens, and that we have developed a model to study the effects of the microbiota on the immune response to pathogens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the microbiome in respiratory health and disease.
understanding the role of the airway microbe in the lung, and the implications of this for the treatment and prevention of respiratory disease.
the effects of airway dysbiosis on the pathogenesis of lung diseases, including cystic fibrosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lung microbiota is a complex, dynamic and important factor that needs to be taken into account in the study of lung disease and its management.
the lung is a dynamic organ that is constantly exposed to environmental stimuli, including microbial stimuli.

we do not know the extent to which the airway microbiome contributes to respiratory disease and that further studies are required to elucidate the role of host–microbiome interactions in respiratory health and disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the airway microbiome is not only a potential contributor to lung disease but also a potential therapeutic target.
we need to consider the airway microbiome as a key component of lung health and disease.
the lung microbiome has an important role in health and disease, and that the airway microbiome is an important component of the gut–lung axis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the airways are a unique environment that is not sterile but instead harbour a complex and unique microbial community that can influence host physiology and pathophysiology.
the lungs harbour a unique microbiota that may be involved in the pathogenesis of lung diseases.
the microbiome should be considered in respiratory research and clinical management of patients.
